subject: radiology
title: Kerley B Lines, Bat Wing Oedema and Deep Sulcus Sign

steps.title: Kerley B lines are thickened septa
steps.tx: **Kerley B lines** are short horizontal white lines, 1 to 2 cm long, reaching the pleura at the lung bases at right angles to it. Each line is one interlobular septum thickened by fluid or cells, the plain film face of septal thickening that high resolution CT shows directly. Smooth symmetric thickening favours pulmonary oedema, while nodular asymmetric thickening favours lymphangitic tumour spread.
steps.say: Kerley B lines are short horizontal white lines, one to two centimetres long, reaching the pleura at the lung bases at right angles to it. steps.title: Stages of cardiac failure on film
steps.tx: **Pulmonary wedge pressure** stages map neatly onto chest film signs. Between 13 and 18 millimetres of mercury blood redistributes to upper lobes, called cephalisation, with an enlarging heart. From 18 to 25 interstitial oedema adds Kerley lines, peribronchial cuffing and hazy central vessels. Above 25 alveolar oedema floods airspaces into fluffy confluent opacity, usually with pleural effusions layering at the bases.

steps.title: Heart failure floods the alveoli
steps.tx: **Cardiogenic oedema** begins when a failing left ventricle raises pulmonary venous pressure until fluid crosses into interstitium and then alveoli. The illustration contrasts a normal alveolus with the flooded, stiff alveolus of acute failure, matching the film progression from septal lines to confluent shadowing. Kerley lines therefore mark the interstitial stage, appearing before airspace flooding makes the patient severely breathless at rest.

steps.title: Peribronchial cuffing and fissure fluid
steps.tx: **Peribronchial cuffing** shows bronchi end on as white rings with thick walls because oedema collects in the loose tissue around airways and vessels. Fluid also fills the fissures, thickening the horizontal fissure line, and blurs central vessel margins that are crisp on a dry film. Together with Kerley lines and upper lobe diversion, cuffing completes the interstitial oedema set even before alveoli flood.

steps.title: Bat wing alveolar oedema
steps.tx: **Bat wing opacity** is confluent alveolar oedema hugging both hila and sparing the lung periphery and apices, named for its winged shape. It floods quickly in acute left ventricular failure, fluid overload and neurogenic oedema after head injury. The spared clear rim at the chest wall separates bat wing oedema from bilateral pneumonia, which more often patches the periphery and shows air bronchograms with fever.

steps.title: Effusions complete the failure picture
steps.tx: **Pleural effusion** in cardiac failure layers first at the bases, blunting costophrenic angles and forming a meniscus that climbs the chest wall. The pictured radiograph shows a dense lower zone opacity with that concave meniscus, typical of fluid rather than collapse. Bilateral effusions with Kerley lines and an enlarged heart make cardiogenic oedema far more likely than infection, guiding diuretic treatment before antibiotics.

steps.title: Deep sulcus sign of pneumothorax
steps.tx: **Deep sulcus sign** betrays a pneumothorax on a supine film, where free air collects at the front and deepens the costophrenic sulcus into a long dark finger. Supine air cannot rise to the apex, so the classic visceral pleural line hides. An abnormally sharp diaphragm outline and a hyperlucent upper abdomen join the clue set, and any one of them earns an erect film or ultrasound before a drain decision.

steps.title: Kerley A and C lines
steps.tx: **Kerley A lines** run longer, 2 to 6 cm, sweeping obliquely from hilum toward the upper lobes without reaching pleura, while Kerley C describes a fine reticular network across both lungs. Examiners ask Kerley B most often because basal horizontal lines touching pleura are unmistakable. All three share one mechanism, thickened interlobular septa, so the letter changes with line length and location, not with the underlying fluid or tumour.
